S081.name: Stress_Related_Maladaptive_Response
S081.description: Emotional or behavioral symptoms appearing in response to an identifiable stressor.

subtypes.With Depressed Mood: Symptoms mainly include low mood, tearfulness, or feelings of hopelessness.
subtypes.With Anxiety: Symptoms mainly include nervousness, worry, jitteriness, or separation anxiety.
subtypes.With Mixed Anxiety and Depressed Mood: A combination of depression and anxiety symptoms appears.
subtypes.With Disturbance of Conduct: Symptoms mainly involve violation of rules, truancy, vandalism, reckless driving, or fighting.
subtypes.With Mixed Disturbance of Emotions and C: Both emotional symptoms (depression, anxiety) and behavioral problems appear together.
subtypes.Unspecified: Maladaptive reactions not classified into the above types (e.g., physical complaints, social withdrawal).

symptom.disease_info: Adjustment Disorder is characterized by the development of emotional or behavioral symptoms in response to an identifiable psychosocial stressor, typically emerging within three months of that stressor. The reaction is considered clinically significant because it is out of proportion to what would be expected given the stressor and/or it causes marked impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning, but it does not meet criteria for another specific mental disorder. Symptoms usually resolve within six months after the stressor or its consequences have ended, though they can persist if the stressor is ongoing, and they often present as changes in mood, anxiety, or conduct. It is distinguished from normal stress reactions by its intensity and functional impact, and from disorders like Major Depressive Disorder or PTSD by its time course, symptom profile, and linkage to a discrete life event or change.

patient.stressor: About five months ago, Brian’s distribution center implemented a major restructuring after a merger, which led to a new warehouse management system, rotating shift changes, and a consolidation of roles that doubled his workload. The chaotic rollout disrupted the predictable routines he relied on, and several of his layout and process suggestions were dismissed, leaving him feeling sidelined despite his expertise. Over the following months he found himself staying late to correct errors, skipping his rec league basketball and museum visits, and struggling to maintain the quiet, methodical rhythm that usually kept him balanced. When his supervisor informally warned him about declining accuracy metrics and he realized he had started avoiding certain tasks and calling out of shifts, he agreed to a referral through the company’s employee assistance program to figure out why he was having so much trouble coping with the changes.
patient.chief_complaint: “Ever since all the changes at work, I feel like I’m reacting badly to everything and I can’t adjust to the new setup no matter how hard I try.”

S081.manifestation: Ever since they rolled out all the new systems and shifts, it feels like my whole fuse is shorter—one small shipping error or last‑minute schedule change can send me into this mix of panic, anger, and wanting to just walk out, and I can’t seem to get myself back to the steady, organized groove I used to have no matter how much I tell myself to suck it up.
